input:
For heat transfer, the analogy essentially takes the same form, with the heat-transfer factor occupying the place of $j_D$. The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the heat-transfer factor equal to $f/2$ for the same flow, based on the same underlying boundary-layer argument: namely, that the layer which resists the flow also resists the passage of heat. A short check using measured friction data illustrates how the analogy works in practice. At a Reynolds number of 45000 in a smooth tube, the measured value of $f$ is 0.0056, which means that $f/2$ comes out at 0.0028. A heat-transfer factor that is obtained from measured temperature differences should therefore lie close to that value wherever the conditions of the analogy are satisfied.

Radiation represents one important boundary of those conditions. The analogy is constructed around the convective exchange taking place at the wall; in situations where a substantial proportion of the heat is transferred by radiation, as happens with a hot surface facing cooler surroundings, the total transfer will exceed the convective part that the analogy is able to estimate. In such cases the friction factor effectively checks only the convective share, and a heat-transfer factor calculated from the total duty will stand above $f/2$, without this implying any failure of the measurements on either side.

The friction factor is the measured quantity in the check; the transfer factor is the quantity inferred.
